title: Fraunhofer opens research centre in Braunschweig - electrive.com
content:
The Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft has inaugurated the new Center for Energy Storage and Systems (ZESS) in Braunschweig. The federal government and the state have invested nearly €50 million euros in the research hub, which focuses on solid-state batteries, cell production, and hydrogen technologies, among other areas.
Fraunhofer opens ZESS for battery and hydrogen research in Braunschweig.
Image: Fraunhofer IST
The centre provides approximately 1,750 square metres of laboratory space and a 450 square metre dry room on a total of around 3,300 square metres. The infrastructure is designed for the development of next-generation solid-state batteries and innovative hydrogen technologies.
The German federal government and the state of Lower Saxony have jointly invested around €49.85 million in the new building. The centre aims to more closely integrate research and industrial application, accelerating the scaling and commercialisation of new technologies.
At the ZESS, the Fraunhofer Institute for Surface Engineering and Thin Films IST, the Fraunhofer Institute for Manufacturing Technology and Advanced Materials IFAM, and the Fraunhofer Institute for Ceramic Technologies and Systems IKTS pool their expertise. In the battery sector, their approach spans new materials, production processes, sustainability, and the circular economy.
A key focus is on solid-state batteries. The ZESS is meant to not only investigate new cell chemistries and manufacturing processes in the laboratory but also advance their industrial scalability.
Fraunhofer ZESS examines the battery process chain
“At the Fraunhofer ZESS, we consider the entire process chain – from new materials, through production technologies, and on to sustainability and the circular economy,” said Christoph Herrmann, Director of the Fraunhofer IST and spokesperson for the ZESS. Through combining expertise, the hope is that solid-state batteries and hydrogen technologies will be developed for industrial applications.
The centre is also closely integrated into the research environment of the
TU Braunschweig
. This includes, among others, the Battery LabFactory Braunschweig and the Center for Circular Production of Next Batteries and Fuel Cells. The goal is to create a regional network for battery and fuel cell research as well as industrial technology transfer.
In parallel, Fraunhofer is expanding its international battery research. At the beginning of October, the
Fraunhofer Battery Alliance agreed with partners from South Korea
on closer collaboration in battery materials, cell production, and recycling. While the FFB in Münster primarily addresses the near-series scaling of cell and production technologies, the ZESS in Braunschweig additionally focuses on solid-state batteries and hydrogen technologies.
Fraunhofer has also prioritised sustainability in the building itself. The research facility was constructed as a wood-hybrid structure with reduced concrete usage. Photovoltaic systems on the roof and façade, green roofs, and multifunctional research spaces are designed to lower energy demand and facilitate adaptation to new research priorities in future.

title: carbmee Applies AI-Native Data Foundation to the EU Digital Battery Passport Challenge - Batteries News
content:
carbmee Applies AI-Native Data Foundation to the EU Digital Battery Passport Challenge
As manufacturers face roughly 80 required data fields per battery across fragmented systems, carbmee positions AI-powered data modelling as the path to passport readiness at scale ahead of the 18 February 2027 deadline.
Carbmee, the environmental intelligence company, is applying its AI-native data foundation to one of the hardest problems in the
EU Digital Battery Passport
: assembling verified, product-level data at scale from information scattered across ERP, PLM, MES, supplier portals, spreadsheets, LCA tools, and battery management systems.
Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, from 18 February 2027, EV, light transport, and industrial batteries above 2 kWh require a Digital Battery Passport covering six data categories: general battery and manufacturer information, material composition and sourcing, performance and durability, sustainability and environmental impact, safety, and end-of-life and recycling. Each passport rests on roughly 80 data fields that must be verified, access-tiered, and kept current as a battery moves through use, repair, repurposing, and recycling.
Carbmee’s approach begins with the transactional data a company already holds, then uses AI to connect and model it into a single foundation rather than requiring complete supplier data before any passport can be built. Where primary data is missing, the platform helps teams identify gaps, engage the right suppliers, and validate inputs, so companies can avoid defaulting to high proxy values and the higher assumed emissions that follow.
Because battery passport data is dynamic, updating as service events, state of health, and end-of-life status change, Carbmee’s model is built to maintain lifecycle records over time rather than produce a one-time snapshot. The company argues this is the difference between a claim a manufacturer can defend once and one it can defend continuously.
Carbmee is clear that no software makes a claim lawful and that legal sign-off remains with a company’s counsel. What an AI-native data foundation provides is the verified, auditable, continuously updated data that every passport depends on.
About Carbmee
Carbmee helps enterprise manufacturers reduce cost, risk, and carbon by embedding real-time environmental intelligence into core business systems. The carbmee EIS™ platform manages 5.8 Gt CO2e and delivers, for its customers, an average 345% operational ROI with break-even in four months.

title: Honda Introduces In-Motion Charging Technology for Commercial EVs
content:
Charging
EV Batteries
Automotive & Mobility
Battery Applications
Discover how Honda's wireless charging roads for EVs highlight the power of collaboration and real-world testing to advance sustainable mobility solutions.
October 7, 2026
3 Min Read
Receiver unit compatible with high power density such as large commercial EVs.
Wireless power transfer (WPT) is helping drive the transition to electric vehicles (EVs). By enabling vehicles to charge without physical connections, WPT systems can address key challenges in EV adoption, including charging convenience,
charging infrastructure limitations
, and operational efficiency. For large commercial vehicles that require significant power and often operate tight schedules, in-motion
wireless charging
could be particularly impactful, reducing downtime and improving the productivity of commercial EV fleets.
Honda R&D Co., Ltd., in partnership with Taisei Corporation and Taisei Rotec Corporation, has developed a wireless power transfer (WPT) road system designed to enable in-motion charging of electric vehicles (EVs). This initiative, which focuses on large commercial vehicles, aims to address key challenges in EV adoption while preparing for real-world implementation through extensive testing and collaboration.
Related:
EV Charging Demand Outpaces Infrastructure Growth, Signaling Market Shift for Charge Station Operators
Addressing the needs of large commercial vehicles
Unlike many wireless charging systems that primarily target passenger EVs, Honda’s WPT road system is specifically designed to meet the demands of large commercial vehicles. The companies' collaboration has developed the underlying technology for a magnetic-coupling wireless power transfer road system (“WPT road system”). Commercial vehicles, which can weigh up to 20 tons, require robust infrastructure that can handle high power loads and ensure long-term durability.
Key roles of the three companies in this joint research. Courtesy of Honda.
The system combines proprietary technology from each company: a Honda high-power-density power receiver/transmitter unit compatible with DC power distribution; a Taisei high-response DC power supply system; and Taisei Rotec technology for embedding equipment in roads.
This focus on commercial applications is particularly significant for the logistics and transportation sectors, where operational efficiency is critical. Frequent charging stops can disrupt schedules and increase costs. Honda’s in-motion charging system aims to reduce the need for stationary charging, allowing vehicles to operate more efficiently. As noted in Honda’s press release, “DWPT technology is expected to enhance the convenience of EVs by supplying power to vehicles while they are in motion, thereby reducing the frequency of charging needed at home or at charging stations.”
DC distribution-based GA system, easily embedded in roads. Courtesy of Honda.
Real-world testing and practical implementation
Starting in Japan’s 2027 fiscal year, the three companies plan to conduct demonstration testing of the WPT road system on public roads. This follows extensive validation testing at Taisei Group’s Future Technology Field (T-FIELD/SATTE), where the system’s durability and performance were evaluated under conditions simulating heavy commercial vehicle traffic.
Related:
These 10 Countries have the Most Charging Power per EV
The public road testing will focus on verifying the system’s ability to deliver high-power wireless charging at speeds suitable for large commercial vehicles. Honda aims to achieve power output levels of up to 150 kW, ensuring the system can meet the demands of high-speed logistics operations. The testing will also evaluate long-term durability, electromagnetic field leakage, and the reliability of power transfer performance. Honda emphasized, “Through these tests, the three companies will strive to ensure both power transfer performance and the safety of the ground assembly (GA) units as structures embedded in the roadway.”
A step toward sustainable mobility
Honda’s focus on large commercial vehicles and its dedication to practical testing reflect its broader vision for sustainable mobility. By addressing the unique challenges of the logistics and transportation sectors, this technology aims to enhance the convenience and efficiency of EVs.
Related:
Could AI Help In-Flight Drone Recharging Take Off?
As Honda stated, “Striving to realize a sustainable mobility society where people can enjoy freedom of mobility well into the future, Honda will continue to pursue co-creation with a diverse range of partners beyond the automotive industry, including road infrastructure-related businesses, government agencies, and energy-related businesses.” This initiative represents a step forward in developing EV infrastructure, with the potential to support the widespread adoption of EVs in both commercial and passenger applications. Once again, it has been demonstrated that collaboration is key to technology innovation.

title: Bosch Sees Multi-Powertrain Future for Trucks
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Design & Manufacturing
Bosch abandons bridge metaphor for multi-lane highway, embracing combustion, hybrid & electric truck configurations.
October 6, 2026
At a Glance
Bosch rejects the assumption that the commercial vehicle market will converge on one powertrain.
The company describes powertrain diversity as a multi-lane highway rather than a transitional bridge.
Software and sensors define the truck of the future as much as propulsion systems do, Bosch says.
Bosch Mobility Americas
president and CEO Paul Thomas addressed the press at the company's Mobility Experience Days event at its Flat Rock, MI proving grounds.
The company has previously exhibited technologies like its
Powernet Guardian
at this event.
He discussed the company's support for the expected variety of powertrain options for future
pickup truck
buyers in his presentation:
"I like to call it the truck of the future. And the truck of the future isn't only defined by what's under the hood. It's defined by how you interact with the vehicle and how the vehicle interacts with the market that it operates in.
And it really depends on what it can do for the people that's driving it. And it's made possible by not only the powertrain or the propulsion, but by the software and the sensors that are included in the vehicle and the way they interact with the vehicle itself and with the environment that it operates in.
So let me walk you through, at least in my mind, what that looks like in practice. The old assumption was that the market moves in one direction towards a dominant powertrain, and that really doesn't match what we're seeing in the market today, or what the customers are buying, and what we see in our data. So our answer from Bosch is that there is no single winning powertrain.
Over the past couple of years, I've always said this: that we want to have a focus on all technologies, whether it be internal combustion engines, whether it be hybrids, or whether it be electrified mobility, we believe that there is a multi-lane highway. We used to describe it as a bridge from one technology to another, but we thought that was too myopic.
The fact that it's not a bridge. This is a multi-lane highway having multiple choices of powertrain will be there for a while, and there'll be all different types of configurations based upon what each customer wants."

title: DHL: Exploring Top Trends in Global Supply Chains
content:
DHL: Exploring Top Trends in Global Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
DHL explores the core trends driving trade in 2026. Credit: DHL
DHL Express CEO John Pearson explains that AI is the biggest driver of supply chain transformation, with insights from the DHL Globalisation Tracker
Over the last 12 months, trade has undergone significant transformation and disturbance. Much of this can even be dated back to the Covid-19 pandemic.
Periods of AI adoption, tariff implementation and volatility around the world have proven to be a
disruptive force for global logistics
DHL has released the latest edition of the DHL Globalisation Tracker, in collaboration with New York University's Stern School of Business.
The impact of AI
Trade policy has been a major driver of change and disruption in 2026. While
geopolitical conflicts and increasing tariffs
are taking place, organisations around the world are racing to build infrastructure for AI.
The DHL Globalisation Tracker uses more than 30 million data points, analysing the international flow of trade capital, information and people.
Despite the volatility that this year has seen, global goods trade grew faster in H1 2026 than in any half-year in the past 15 years, apart from the Covid rebound. The report found that much of this was due to the increase in demand for AI infrastructure, as semiconductors and data-transmission equipment moved to the top of everyone’s priority list.
The growing demand for reliable AI products has seen an immense growth in semiconductors, with various shortages and backlogs taking place throughout the year. According to WTO and OECD analysis, 42% of goods trade growth in 2025 was driven by trade in AI-enabling goods. In the first quarter of 2026, this rose to 76%. This demonstrates how much of a main commodity this technology is becoming, and how it is shaping modern trade.
“The biggest story in global trade right now is AI – not tariffs,” explains John Pearson, CEO of DHL Express.
“Every AI query ultimately depends on logistics. Chips, networking equipment and the many other goods behind this technology must be in the right place at the right time. DHL connects the businesses and markets behind these
complex supply chains
. Whenever innovation creates new trade flows, our global network helps keep them moving.”
John Pearson, CEO of DHL Express
Key numbers
Globalisation has reached a record level of 25.8%
The US accounted for only 13% of global imports in recent years
Global trade is expected to grow by an average of 3.4% per year through 2029
Trade in AI-enabling goods drove 76% of goods trade growth in Q1 2026
The value of trade fell 37% in Saudi Arabia in the first five months of 2026, compared to the same period in 2025
Risk and logistics
Alongside the AI integration, trade routes have been disrupted by a number of factors. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has proven to be a challenge, resulting in idling ships and journeys that take much longer and cost more money.
However, DHL suggests that the impact was felt in uneven measures. In Saudi Arabia, the value of trade fell 37% and it fell 7% in the United Arab Emirates in the first five months of 2026, compared with 2025 numbers. The economies dependent on the Strait were hit the hardest.
At the same time, trade policy proved its own issue. US tariffs were at a significant high, but
their global impact remained
limited. This was partially due to the fact that the US accounted for only 13% of the world’s imports in recent years.
Out of those 13%, half of the imports were exempt from the tariff increases, due to trade deals that took place in August 2026. Alongside this, rather than retaliating to tariff increases, most countries worked instead to develop new trade agreements and diversify their markets.
Despite recent shocks, however, global goods trade is still expected to grow by an average of 3.4% per year through 2029.
“The surprise is not only that global trade kept growing through new tariffs and the Iran war,” says Prof. Steven A. Altman, Director of the DHL Initiative on Globalisation at NYU Stern’s Center for the Future of Management.
“The outlook is now stronger than it was before either shock. This reminds us to look beyond the most visible disruptions and recognise the deeper reasons why trade remains so resilient. The AI trade boom highlights the demand for goods and services that can only be provided efficiently when specialised producers work together across countries. It also shows how companies continually adapt to keep trade moving through disruptions and policy shifts.”
Prof. Steven A. Altman, Director of the DHL Initiative on Globalisation at NYU Stern’s Center for the Future of Management
Global trade networks
The report found that the strongest trade growth was in East Asia and the Pacific, with a value rise of 24% in the first five months of 2026, compared with the same period the year prior.
This was followed by Europe (12%) and Sub-Saharan Africa (11%).
Aside from trade growth, the East Asia and Pacific region also saw the largest share of domestic trade. In the first five months, the share of trade within the region was at 60%, a growth from 57% the year prior.
Though the
US-China split
was anticipated to have a major impact, the fallout was relatively minimal. At its peak in 2015, trade between the two nations only accounted for 3.5% of the world’s total – this fell to just 1.6% during the first five months of 2026.
While there were fears of alliances and relationships breaking down around the world, many trade relationships have remained the same following the US-China dispute.
Based on international flows of trade, capital, information and people, globalisation reached a record level of 25.8% in 2025. This was partially related to
AI trade and investments
Whenever innovation creates new trade flows, our global network helps keep them moving.
John Pearson, CEO of DHL Express
Trade growth was particularly high in the East Asia and Pacific region. Credit: DHL

title: Levi's & SE Advisory Q&A: Decarbonising Fashion Logistics
content:
Levi's & SE Advisory Q&A: Decarbonising Fashion Logistics
Prioritise Us
on Google
Dave Rimkus and I am Head of Global Supply Chain Decarbonisation at SE Advisory Services and Jennifer DuBuisson, Sr. Director of Sustainability for Levi Strauss & Co. Credit: Levi Strauss & Co
Jennifer DuBuisson and Dave Rimkus on how the Fashion Renewable Collaborative helps suppliers adopt renewable electricity at scale & reduce fragmentation
Levi Strauss & Co and Schneider Electric's
SE Advisory Services
are each advancing supply chain strategies that turn climate ambitions into practical action across their global sourcing and manufacturing networks.
As suppliers face mounting pressure from multiple brand customers and evolving regulatory requirements, both organisations are prioritising measurable reductions in Scope 3 emissions, energy use and supplier engagement while strengthening long-term supply chain resilience.
As Senior Director of Sustainability for Levi Strauss & Co, Jennifer DuBuisson helps shape the company's supply chain sustainability strategy, guiding work that spans supplier energy transition, water stewardship, nature and regulatory engagement and translating strategy into actions that procurement and sourcing teams can implement.
As Head of Global Supply Chain Decarbonisation at SE Advisory Services, Schneider Electric's global consulting practice, Dave Rimkus leads a team that helps organisations design and deliver supplier-facing emissions-reduction programs grounded in the operational realities of textile mills, dye houses and finishing facilities.
Jennifer's work involves collaborating across Levi Strauss & Co to embed sustainability into supplier relationships and sourcing decisions, with a focus on delivering measurable outcomes across the company's global manufacturing value chain.
Dave's work spans measuring supplier carbon footprints, building technical capabilities within supplier organisations and evaluating renewable electricity procurement options, ensuring that corporate emissions targets are backed by actionable steps at the facility level.
Together, Jennifer and Dave collaborated on the launch of the Fashion Renewable Collaborative (FRC) during New York Climate Action Week in September 2026, a landmark supply chain initiative co-founded by Levi Strauss & Co and Marks & Spencer (M&S) with
SE Advisory Services
as global implementation partner.
The FRC is designed to help fashion suppliers adopt renewable electricity at scale by providing digital education, market guidance and practical procurement support, addressing the sector's single largest supply chain decarbonisation lever and reducing the burden of fragmented, brand-by-brand engagement for facilities serving multiple customers.
Jennifer and Dave share their knowledge with Sustainability Magazine, Supply Chain Digital's sister brand.
SE Advisory Services - Expertise. Innovation. Impact.
What is the FRC and what challenges does it address?
The FRC is a joint industry initiative launched by Levi Strauss & Co. and
with SE Advisory Services as the global implementation partner.
The goal is to make it easier for fashion suppliers to understand and adopt renewable electricity at scale.
A large share of
’s emissions come from energy-intensive manufacturing, including textile mills, dye houses and finishing facilities.
But suppliers are often responding to different climate targets and decarbonisation requests from several brand customers at once. Many also face limited resources, financing constraints and energy markets that vary significantly from country to country.
The FRC is designed to reduce some of that fragmentation through a shared, practical model. It provides education, market guidance and implementation support so suppliers can understand their options and pursue credible renewable electricity pathways, whether through onsite generation, energy attribute certificates, green tariffs, storage or power purchase agreements.
The aim is to help suppliers take practical steps, rather than add another commitment to the list.
At NYCAW, SE Advisory Services hosted a panel on how collaboration can accelerate supply chain decarbonisation in the fashion industry. Credit: SE Advisory
How can collaboration help fashion brands translate their climate commitments into measurable emissions reductions?
Collaboration is essential because suppliers do not work for one brand at a time.
They serve multiple customers, often in different markets and can receive overlapping requests that add work without making emissions reductions easier to achieve. A shared approach gives brands a common way to engage suppliers.
Rather than creating separate education programs, assessments and reporting requests, brands can align their support and focus resources where emissions reductions are most achievable. That reduces the burden on suppliers and gives them more practical help to evaluate renewable electricity options.
The FRC builds on work already underway at Levi Strauss & Co. and M&S.
Levi’s LEAP program, developed with SE Advisory Services, helps suppliers in India evaluate renewable electricity options through training, financial analysis and advisory support.
M&S’s RE:Spark program, also developed with SE Advisory Services, gives suppliers access to digital resources, regional market information and guidance on options such as onsite solar, certificates, green tariffs and PPAs.
Together, the programs have registered nearly 500 supplier facilities. SE Advisory Services brings energy-market expertise, advisory support and digital tools, like Resource Advisor+ for Supply Chain, to support supplier onboarding, engagement tracking, readiness assessments and progress monitoring.
Levi Strauss & Co., Marks & Spencer and Schneider Electric launched the Fashion Renewable Collaborative, a pre-competitive programme designed to reduce emissions through aggregated renewable energy purchasing. Credit: SE Advisory
Schneider Electric supports more than 20 supply chain decarbonisation initiatives globally, involving more than 3,100 supplier companies and 16 multi-buyer renewable energy cohorts.
brands do not need to address this challenge alone. By working together, they can give suppliers a more consistent path to renewable electricity adoption and better connect climate commitments with measurable emissions reductions across the supply chain.
Can renewable energy accelerate the fashion industry's decarbonisation and if so, how?
Jennifer:
Renewable electricity is one of the most important levers we have as an industry.
Textile processing accounts for more than half of the apparel industry's emissions and shifting to renewable electricity represents roughly two-thirds of the sector's identified decarbonisation potential. The challenge isn't supplier willingness; it's complexity and economics.
When we launched our Levi's Energy Accelerator Program (LEAP) last year with Schneider Electric to help our suppliers in India adopt renewable electricity, nearly 50 suppliers registered in the first year. Once we reduced the friction, the demand was there.
We also learned that the barriers are local, so suppliers need guidance specific to where they are, support in their own language and a range of options, from power purchase agreements and energy attribute certificates to on-site generation and storage.
Most importantly, we saw that no single brand can solve this alone. Suppliers often field nearly identical requests from multiple brands.
That's why we co-founded the FRC with M&S and Schneider Electric: to give suppliers one clear, coordinated path to renewable electricity, rather than many different versions of the same ask.
And by aggregating supplier demand, we can improve project economics, making renewable electricity more competitive with other investment priorities.
Introducing the Levi's® Wear Longer Project
Renewable electricity adoption is one of the biggest opportunities to reduce emissions in fashion manufacturing, especially in energy-intensive parts of the supply chain.
The World Resources Institute and Apparel Impact Institute estimate that moving manufacturing to renewable electricity represents roughly two-thirds of the sector’s identified emissions-reduction potential.
Textile processing alone accounts for more than half of apparel industry emissions. When a mill or dye house lowers the carbon intensity of the electricity it uses, it can make a meaningful difference to a brand’s Scope 3 footprint. There is no single solution for every supplier.
The right approach depends on where a facility is located, its electricity demand profile, local regulations, available contract structures and its ability to invest.
Onsite solar may work in one market, while a green tariff, energy attribute certificate or power purchase agreement may be a better fit elsewhere. Suppliers need clear information and commercial support to evaluate those choices.
In some cases, aggregating demand can also give smaller suppliers access to renewable electricity procurement opportunities they could not pursue on their own.
What does sustainability and decarbonisation look like at Levi's?
Jennifer:
Levi Strauss & Co. was built on a product designed to last and that idea has shaped how we've innovated for more than 170 years.
Today, our work focuses on three areas: climate, consumption and community.
On climate, our science-based targets establish the destination and our Climate Transition Plan serves as the roadmap, with a strong focus on our supply chain where the greatest impact lies.
Jennifer and Dave at NYCAW after announcing the Fashion Renewable Collaborative. Credit: SE Advisory
That includes our commitment to transition to low carbon fuels from our supply chain by 2030 as a UN Fashion Industry Charter for Climate Action signatory and initiatives like the FRC to accelerate renewable electricity adoption.
We've also collaborated with financial partners to help suppliers access lower-cost capital tied to their sustainability performance, recognising that accelerating investment often requires a combination of financial, technical and operational support.
On water, our 2030 strategy commits to a 15% absolute reduction in water use across our manufacturing supply chain and for 40% of the water used in manufacturing to be recycled or reused.
Across all of this, our approach is the same: bring peers and suppliers together around collective, measurable action that can scale.
Do you think there are other ways that fashion can become more sustainable and can you share your ideas?
Jennifer:
Companies of course play the biggest role, but consumers are part of the solution, too.
Only 59% of young people can sew a button, patch a hole or alter a hem, compared to 79% of older generations.
Our Wear Longer Project teaches these repair skills and has reached nearly 90,000 students, most recently through after-school programming in New York City public schools.
Buying something that lasts, caring for it and repairing it when needed remains one of the most effective things any of us can do.
The best way to reduce your impact is to wear what you love, longer.
Collaborating with Levi Strauss & Co
Levi’s and
Racing have joined forces on a seven-piece collection inspired by vintage racing cars, combining motorsport heritage with classic denim styles and contemporary design.
Levi’s and
have collaborated on a collection combining denim craftsmanship with performance-inspired design, including Air Max 95 trainers, trucker jackets and baggy jeans.

Levi’s and Barbour have brought together their workwear heritage in a collaborative collection of waxed jackets, denim outerwear and other garments designed to celebrate craftsmanship, durability and timeless style.

title: This e-bike fits seven riders, and that’s not even the craziest thing about it
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 7 2026 - 8:26 am PT
If you’ve ever looked at a cargo e-bike and thought, “Sure, but where am I supposed to put the other six people?”, SixThreeZero may finally have the answer.
The company’s latest addition to its growing e-bike and e-trike lineup, the
Long Range Luxury Rickshaw
, is already a fairly ridiculous machine in its standard form. It combines three wheels, dual motors, rear passenger seating bench, and enough battery capacity to make many electric motorcycles jealous. But start adding its optional passenger trailers, and you can essentially build yourself a seven-person electric bicycle train.
And somehow, that’s still not the craziest number on the spec sheet.
The rickshaw packs a whopping 7,300 Wh of battery capacity. That’s not a typo. We didn’t move a decimal. It’s literally got 10x the battery capacity of most e-bikes.
The setup includes two 48V 20Ah batteries integrated into the frame, plus an enormous 48V 112Ah battery mounted beneath the rear passenger seat. Combined, that works out to 7,296 Wh of capacity.
For comparison, a typical commuter e-bike might have a 500-750 Wh battery.
The company claims up to 120 miles (193 km) of range, though as always, actual range will depend heavily on speed, terrain, assist level, and – perhaps more than with most e-bikes – how many friends you’ve talked into joining your bicycle conga line.
But with that mileage figure working out to an efficiency of around 60 Wh/mi (36 Wh/km), that spec sheet range number might actually be a fairly realistic rating. There are a lot of e-bike companies trying to claim 100-mile ranges with a 720 Wh battery, though they admittedly don’t have the rolling resistance of this e-trike locomotive.
Power comes from a pair of 750W motors. Riders can select single or dual-motor operation, with the latter offering 1,500W of combined nominal power for hills and heavy loads. Top speed is listed at 20 mph (32 km/h), available through either pedal assist or throttle.
The base rickshaw seats the rider plus two rear passengers and starts at
a rather hefty $7,495
. But that’s where things get interesting.
SixThreeZero offers $999 rear “sub-frames” that attach behind the trike, with options for passenger seating or cargo baskets. Up to two can apparently be connected, creating the seven-person configuration pictured above.
There are even powered versions of those sub-frames with their own motor and battery, controlled from the cockpit of the main bike. At that point, we’re getting dangerously close to building a Mad Max electric road train one bicycle component at a time.
Other equipment includes hydraulic disc brakes on all three wheels, a torque sensor, 20 x 4-inch fat tires, suspension fork, ergonomic handlebars, headlights with high and low beams, turn signals, mirrors, brake lights, a rear differential, and a front cargo basket.
Oh, and a captain’s chair that looks significantly better than the seats in my first car.
Electrek’s Take
Is a $7,495 three-wheeled e-bike with more than 7 kWh of batteries and a pair of passenger trailers excessive? Absolutely.
But I’m also having trouble pretending I don’t want to load six friends aboard and find out just how far this wonderfully absurd contraption can actually go.
And having
personally tested SixThreeZero Rickshaws in the past
, including putting at least six people on one (pictured below), I know they make these things well.
Lord help the first guy who ever tries to back one of these e-bike trains up, though.
Definitely don’t try this at home. But if you do, follow my lead and use borrowed kids from around the neighborhood

title: Rivian R2 gets live Pet Cam in update, AI assistant, and more
content:
Rivian R2
Fred Lambert
| Oct 7 2026 - 8:25 am PT
Rivian is rolling out Pet Cam, a new feature in software update 2026.36 that lets R2 owners check on a pet left in the vehicle through a live video feed in the Rivian app.
It’s exclusive to the R2. R1T and R1S owners get new remote Pet Mode controls instead, and the same update brings the Rivian Assistant to the R2, four months after the SUV launched.
How Pet Cam works on the R2
Rivian announced the feature today
. Pet Cam uses the R2’s interior cabin camera, which the company describes as a “high-definition RGB” unit, to send a full-color view of the cabin to your phone.
The Rivian R2. Pet Cam relies on its color cabin camera. Source: Rivian
There are two ways to use it. You can open a live stream from the Gear Guard section of the Rivian app, with a badge on the video showing the current cabin temperature. Or you can skip the stream entirely, because the app dashboard and your phone’s lock screen get fresh still images of the cabin on a regular basis.
Pet Cam sits in the Gear Guard tile of the Rivian app. Source: Rivian
Most of the time, you don’t want to watch your dog sleep for five minutes. You want a two-second look to confirm everything is fine, and a lock screen snapshot with the temperature on it does that without opening anything.
Rivian also built in an off switch. Anyone sitting in the vehicle can end the live stream with one tap on the center display.
The automaker says more than 60% of its owners travel with a dog, which explains why this got done four months into the R2’s life.
Rivian says more than 60% of its owners travel with a dog. Source: Rivian
R1T and R1S get app controls, no camera
R1 owners aren’t getting Pet Cam. Rivian ties the feature to the R2’s cabin camera and didn’t announce a version for its flagship truck and SUV.
What Gen 1 and Gen 2 R1 owners do get is remote control of Pet Mode, which the R2 gets too. Until now, you had to turn Pet Mode on before you left the vehicle. With 2026.36, you can switch it on from the Rivian app after you’ve walked away, and switch it off by tapping the paw icon in the app’s climate controls.
Either way, the app asks you to confirm first. That’s there so you don’t shut off the climate control by accident, or leave it running for hours.
Pet Mode on the R2’s center display. Source: Rivian
The catch is Connect+
Rivian’s announcement doesn’t mention pricing. But there’s a catch.
Rivian’s own Connect+ page lists “remote camera livestreaming” as a paid feature, not a standard one. Connect+ costs $14.99 a month or $149.99 a year.
The fine print on that page also caps Gear Guard Live Cam at one hour of streaming per day. It says interior viewing only works with Pet Mode enabled and “is not to be used for people.”
Tesla owners will find all of this familiar.
Tesla launched Dog Mode in 2019
, and its owner’s manual says you can view the cabin from the Tesla app while the mode is on, with periodic cabin snapshots on newer iPhones. Tesla’s
remote live camera view launched as a Premium Connectivity feature
, and that plan costs $9.99 a month.
Rivian Assistant reaches the R2
Update 2026.36 also brings Rivian’s AI voice assistant to the R2. It can adjust climate, media and navigation, answer general questions, pull up the weather at your destination, and identify the song that’s playing.
You call it up by pressing the right Haptic Halo Wheel on the steering wheel, tapping an icon on the display, or saying “Hey, Rivian.”
Rivian Assistant on the R2’s center display. Source: Rivian
R1 owners have had it since May. When
Rivian launched the “Hey Rivian” assistant
, we reported that it would be on the R2 when customer deliveries started. The
R2 launched on June 9
, so buyers waited four months for a feature that was supposed to be there on day one. And it needs Connect+ too.

title: E-bikes are causing a surprising new problem in Europe
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 7 2026 - 7:36 am PT
Europe has spent years encouraging people to ditch cars and get around on bicycles and e-bikes instead. And in many places, it’s working. But all of those increasingly sophisticated electric bicycles have created an unexpected new problem: there aren’t nearly enough people to fix them.
Europe could need to recruit a staggering 105,000 additional bicycle mechanics by 2032, according to a new report on the continent’s cycling industry.
The NextGen Mechanics report, presented at the inaugural European Cycling Industries (ECI) summit in Brussels, estimates that Europe currently has around 175,000 bicycle mechanics. But
Bike Europe
says the industry is already short around 45,000 workers, and growing adoption of e-bikes, cargo bikes, bike leasing, and commercial cycling fleets is expected to make that shortage significantly worse.
And e-bikes are a big part of the reason why.
Modern electric bicycles increasingly require more than the traditional assortment of hex keys that can solve most issues on a good-old-fashioned ten-speed. E-bikes can require electrical troubleshooting, firmware diagnostics, motor servicing, battery expertise, and specialized training that varies between manufacturers.
Cargo bikes add another layer of complexity (especially since nearly all cargo bikes sold in Europe
are now equipped with electric motors
), while growing fleets of rental, delivery, and leased e-bikes mean many bikes are accumulating mileage much faster than the average privately owned bicycle.
The result is that workshops simply can’t keep up.
According to Shimano’s State of the Nation 2026 survey, 212 million Europeans experience some type of barrier when trying to maintain their bicycles. The report says 121 million people consequently ride less often, while 7.6 million have stopped cycling altogether due to service delays.
That last figure is particularly troubling. After all, an e-bike doesn’t do much
to replace a car
if it’s sitting in a garage for six weeks waiting for someone to diagnose a motor error.
The problem isn’t simply a lack of people interested in working on bikes, either. The report points toward relatively low wages, poor career prospects, and fragmented training systems as major contributors.
Low pay and low social status were cited by 72% of respondents as factors behind the shortage. In Germany, for example, bicycle mechanics earn an average of around €30,000 per year compared to a national average salary of €43,000. In Italy and Spain, average mechanic salaries are reportedly just €16,000 per year.
Meanwhile, training varies wildly between European countries. Germany, Austria, and Switzerland have established apprenticeship systems, while other countries rely on vocational programs, dealer training, or largely informal pathways into the industry.
ECI is now proposing a standardized pan-European entry-level qualification that would include mechanical skills as well as electrical diagnostics and safety training, with manufacturer-specific education layered on top.
Electrek’s Take
I’m going to go out on a limb here and call this one of the better problems for the cycling industry to have.
The rapid growth of e-bikes has created an entire new category of skilled technical jobs, and now the biggest issue is figuring out how to train enough people and pay them well enough to stick around. At lot of us – myself included – can talk in the past tense about the time we spent working in a bike shop. For many of us, it was a temporary job as a springboard to something else, and the number of folks who stick around is seriously lacking. The industry needs more qualified bike mechanics and it needs them yesterday.
We shouldn’t underestimate how serious the problem can become, as it directly impacts bikes’ ability to continue improving cities. As e-bikes increasingly replace cars for commuting, school runs, deliveries, and other daily transportation, reliable service becomes much more important. If your recreational mountain bike spends two weeks in the shop, that’s really annoying. If your cargo e-bike that you use to take two kids to school every morning spends two weeks in the shop, you’ve suddenly got a transportation problem.
And the increasing technical complexity of e-bikes means the old model of simply hiring someone who is good with bikes isn’t necessarily enough anymore. These are becoming increasingly sophisticated vehicles, and the people maintaining them need the training – and compensation – that reflects that.
Perhaps the biggest takeaway here isn’t that Europe somehow has “too many e-bikes.” It’s that the rest of the cycling ecosystem hasn’t grown fast enough to support them.

title: Hyundai shelves IONIQ 3 launch in Australia as cheaper Chinese EVs take over
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 7 2026 - 6:50 am PT
has scrapped plans to launch the IONIQ 3 in Australia. Importing the electric hatch would be too costly to compete with low-priced Chinese EVs.
Hyundai cancels the IONIQ 3 for Australia
The IONIQ 3 will not go on sale in Australia as Hyundai initially planned. Hyundai announced the electric hatch would arrive in Australia in early 2027, following its launch in Europe and the UK.
That will no longer happen. Hyundai quietly removed the IONIQ 3 landing page from its Australian website.
A company spokesperson confirmed to
that bringing the IONIQ 3 to Australia, which is built in Turkey, would be “too difficult” and costly.
“The cost of importation is high, and the car will be fighting in a very price-sensitive segment. The numbers just don’t work for us given the competition,” Hyundai’s spokesperson explained.
The IONIQ 3 was expected to go on sale in Australia priced from around AUD$40,000, before on-road costs. Unlike other Hyundai and Kia models, Hyundai produces the IONIQ 3 at its Izmit plant in Turkey, which would make it too expensive to compete with lower-priced Chinese EVs.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 N-Line (Source: Hyundai UK)
According to
The Driven
, the top 10 best-selling electric vehicles in Australia through September include the Tesla Model Y (35,930), BYD Sealion 7 (19,964), Geely EX5 (12,745), Zeekr 7X (10,800), Omoda Jaecoo J5 (10,664), BYD Atto 2 (8,673), Tesla Model 3 (5,775), Kia EV5 (4,722), Kia EV3 (4,541), and BYD Atto 1 (4,471).
The IONIQ 3 would have competed against others in the segment, such as BYD’s Dolphin, which starts at as low as AUD$28,888.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 (Source: Hyundai UK)
In the UK, the IONIQ 3 is
now on sale
, starting at just £18,495 ($25,000) OTR, including the £3,750 Electric Car Grant. In Europe, it costs around €28,950 ($33,000).
Hyundai’s electric hatch is available with 42 kWh and 61 kWh battery packs. The base IONIQ 3 Advance trim with the 42 kWh battery offers up to 213 miles of WLTP range. The IONIQ 3 Advance with the 61 kWh battery starts at £21,995 ($29,000) and offers a “class-leading” WLTP range of up to 308 miles.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 interior with Pleos Connect infotainment system (Source: Hyundai)
The IONIQ 3 is also Hyundai’s first vehicle in Europe equipped with its new Pleos Connect infotainment system.
Measuring 4,155 mm (163.5″) long, 1,800 mm (70.9″) wide, and 1,505 mm (59.3″) high, with a 2,680 mm (105.5″) wheelbase, the IONIQ 3 is slightly smaller than the Kia EV3.

title: E-quipment highlight: AMT's hot-swapping battery electric rail excavator
content:
Commercial EVs
Electric Heavy Machinery
Jo Borrás
| Oct 7 2026 - 5:42 am PT
Rarely seen by the general public,
rail road excavators are a critical piece of the infrastructure puzzle
– one that can travel directly on the tracks while digging, lifting, and clearing obstacles from the track, working on everything from track maintenance and renewal to utility and civil construction projects. This one’s electric.
Co-developed by Dutch equipment brand AMT and construction firm Royal BAM, the TW series of electric rail road excavators (available in 150, 160, and 180 sizes, representing 18-24 metric tonne classes) are all-electric machines packing a 600V electrical system managing a water-cooled, permanent-magnet electric motor putting out 121 kW (~160 hp).
The motor draws power from a set of four 90 kWh battery packs (360 kWh total) good for 8-16 hours of continuous operation. The interesting bit, though, is not only that the batteries are swappable to help the excavator keep on keepin’ on – they’re hot swappable, meaning it can keep working on two or three batteries while a second machine plucks one out and pops in another one,
so the crew can keep riding the rails
What’s more, the same modular 90 kWh battery packs can be shared across a number of AMT machines, which keeps energy from being stranded in idle assets and reduces the job’s total investment in batteries and machinery in the same way – and for the same reasons – that similar systems work for
Craftsman
Milwaukee
Hot swap, won’t stop
The clever battery-swap trick doesn’t mean AMT treated charging as an afterthought, though. The excavator’s onboard charger can charge the batteries at up to 120 kW, which the company claims can bring the full 260 kW pack from a 20–80% SOC in under two hours – so you won’t need three or four machines to make the battery pack investment make sense.
You can check out some of the AMT electric rail excavator’s specs
in the company’s online brochure

title: Toyo cuts the ribbon on its newly-expanded solar factory in Texas - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Company officers and government officials celebrated the 2 GW expansion of Toyo’s Humble, Texas solar module facility and looked forward to planned heterojunction cell production at the site in 2028.
Ben Zientara
07 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
In a ceremony that featured appearances from U.S. and foreign dignitaries alongside company executives and industry professionals, Japanese solar manufacturer Toyo Co., Ltd celebrated the expansion of its Humble, Texas solar module assembly plant on Tuesday.
The facility, which first became operational in Oct. 2025, now boasts 2 GW of annual module capacity. The company plans a $357 million expansion of the site to include a 1.5 GW heterojunction (HJT) solar cell manufacturing line it expects to be operational by Q1 2028. By that time, the plant is expected to host a workforce of 400 employees.
Toyo currently manufactures solar cells at a 4 GW facility in Hawassa, Ethiopia and a 2 GW factory in Vietnam.
Jeffrey Kessler, U.S. under secretary of commerce for industry and security joined in the ceremony to celebrate the company’s domestic investments. “Toyo’s announcement is the direct result of the Trump Administration’s bold policies to bring manufacturing and jobs back to America,” he said in a comment. “By investing hundreds of millions of dollars to expand its Texas factory, onshoring overseas production, and committing to use exclusively US polysilicon, Toyo is making an important contribution to America’s manufacturing renaissance.”
The company was also joined by solar industry veteran Paul Wormser, senior vice president of Intertek CEA. Shortly before the ribbon cutting event, Toyo
announced the results
of an Intertek CEA factory audit, the outcome of which the company described as “a strong result.”
Wormser went further in a comment, stating “Our team conducts a rigorous, independent review of every element of a factory’s operations — quality systems, processes, and risk controls. We check a thousand different things in twelve major areas. And in those twelve major areas, we have never found perfection, but Toyo has gotten our highest grade.”
Immediately preceding the event, Toyo held an “Analyst Day” webinar in which the company described its recent financial performance and plans for the near term.
During the call, Toyo executives discussed the planned buildout of the company’s domestic cell line (currently in the permitting and approvals stage), and its response to the Ethiopia circumvention inquiry initiated by the U.S. Department of Commerce in July, 2026, which followed from
a petition filed in May
The inquiry seeks to determine whether cells made using Chinese silicon wafers illegally circumvent import tariffs on Chinese solar products. Toyo says it is seeking clarification on whether its cells — which it says are made using wafers produced in Indonesia from mostly U.S. polysilicon — will be subject to penalties if Commerce finds that circumvention has occurred.
The company says it hopes for product-coverage guidance from the Commerce Department, or, at the very least a path to certification of cells for companies that can provide production, sourcing and shipment data that show non-Chinese sources for materials.

title: Solar and storage accounted for nearly 1 million EU jobs in 2025 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Solar and battery storage supported 982,000 jobs in the EU in 2025, with PV accounting for 874,000 positions. Solar employment is expected to decline by 2030 as deployment slows, despite growth in operations, maintenance, manufacturing and recycling jobs.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
07 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
The solar PV and battery storage sectors supported 982,000 full-time equivalent (FTE) jobs in the European Union in 2025, according to SolarPower Europe’s new EU Solar Jobs Report 2026. Solar accounted for 874,000 jobs, while battery energy storage systems (BESS) – included in the association’s study for the first time – accounted for another 108,000.
Employment was driven by deployment growth. The EU added 69 GW of solar capacity in 2025, while battery installations reached 27 GWh. Of all solar and storage jobs, 44% were direct positions and 56% were indirect jobs linked to supply chains and related activities.
Solar employment rose 1% year on year to 874,000 FTEs. Installation and deployment accounted for 742,000 jobs, or 85% of the total. Operations and maintenance reached a record 78,000 jobs, while manufacturing accounted for around 37,000, or just 4% of solar employment, with inverter production representing 90% of manufacturing jobs.
Germany was the EU’s largest solar employment market, with approximately 165,000 FTEs, followed closely by Spain. Italy ranked third, with around 85,000 jobs. Together, the three countries accounted for nearly half of EU solar employment.
The report also points to a shift in market structure. For the first time since the report series began in 2021, utility-scale PV slightly overtook rooftop solar in employment, accounting for 50.2% of jobs.
A similar shift toward larger projects occurred in storage. Utility-scale systems accounted for more than half of new battery capacity installed in 2025 and generated nearly half of deployment-related jobs.
Fewer installation jobs, more in O&M and recycling
SolarPower Europe expects EU solar employment to fall to 766,000 FTEs by 2030, from 874,000 in 2025. The decline will be concentrated in deployment, where employment is projected to fall 22% as annual installations stabilize and productivity improves.
The projected decline in employment will come despite continued growth in the EU solar fleet. SolarPower Europe expects installed capacity to rise from 411 GW in 2025 to 739 GW in 2030. As a result, operations and maintenance employment is projected to increase from 78,000 to 109,000 FTEs.
Manufacturing employment could also increase, reaching 49,000 jobs if announced industrial projects are realized. Jobs in decommissioning and recycling are projected to nearly double, from 16,000 to 30,000 FTEs.
Deployment’s share of solar employment is therefore expected to fall from 85% in 2025 to 76% in 2030. Manufacturing, operations and maintenance, and decommissioning and recycling would collectively account for nearly one-quarter of solar jobs.
The report identifies several priorities for 2026, including maintaining solar skills within industrial and labor policies, improving SME access to training funding, updating training programs to include digital and technical skills, and implementing the training and installation requirements of the revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III).
SolarPower Europe also calls for greater coordination between European training programs and for skills development spanning solar, storage, grids, heat pumps and e-mobility. It recommends expanding apprenticeships, career guidance and pathways for workers transitioning into the sector.

title: AuroraCell launches 9.7 kWh sodium-ion chromium oxide residential battery - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The 48 V residential energy storage system uses sodium-ion NCO chemistry and offers 9.7 kWh of rated energy. AuroraCell claims a cycle life of 20,000 cycles at 100% depth of discharge and backs the battery with a 20-year warranty.
Emiliano Bellini
07 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
The AuroraCell RESS system
Bulgaria-based AuroraCell has introduced a 9.7 kWh residential energy storage system based on sodium-ion chromium oxide (NCO) battery technology.
Unlike standard sodium-ion batteries, sodium-ion NCO technology uses a different cathode chemistry designed to improve battery life, stability and performance across a wider temperature range. Sodium ions still carry the charge, while the NCO cathode gives the battery its distinct performance characteristics.
In practical terms, the system is designed to compensate for some of the typical limitations associated with sodium-ion batteries, including lower energy density and performance constraints at temperature extremes. AuroraCell says its NCO chemistry addresses these trade-offs by prioritizing long cycle life, thermal stability and operation across a broad temperature range, characteristics that are particularly relevant for stationary energy storage applications.
The AuroraCell 9.7 kWh – 48 V RESS Pack is a standalone residential battery designed for use with 48 VDC hybrid inverters. The system has 9.744 kWh of rated energy, a nominal capacity of 210 Ah and a nominal voltage of 46.4 V. Its operating voltage range is 32 V to 54.4 V.
According to AuroraCell, the sodium-ion NCO cells can achieve 20,000 cycles at 100% depth of discharge (DoD) at 25 C.
The battery has a standard and maximum charge rate of 0.5C and a standard discharge rate of 0.5C. Maximum discharge current is 150 A between 0 C and 60 C, while the specified discharge temperature range extends from -40 C to 60 C. Charging is permitted between 0 C and 60 C, according to the manufacturer.
AuroraCell says the system’s sodium-ion NCO architecture provides an ultra-safe design with “no fire and explosion,” without providing further details. The company’s technical literature lists UL9540A, UN38.3, MSDS and CE among the battery’s certifications.
The IP65-rated unit measures 483 mm × 254 mm × 754 mm and weighs 110.5 kg. It supports modular parallel connections, enabling installers to increase storage capacity for larger residential systems, according to the company.
AuroraCell says the 48 V sodium-ion NCO battery is compatible with hybrid inverter platforms from Victron Energy, Deye, Solis, Growatt, Schneider Electric, SMA, Sungrow, Sofar Solar, Studer and Ingeteam. Additional inverter brands can be supported on request.
The new product comes with a 20-year warranty.

title: Thousands of European solar park systems exposed online, say researchers - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Dutch firm Modat and the Netherlands’ cybersecurity agency have identified 8,547 exposed systems at solar and wind sites in 35 European countries, with Spain accounting for more than one-third of the solar total.
Brian Publicover
07 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Researchers from Modat, an internet intelligence company based in The Hague, and the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-NL) of the Netherlands have found 8,547 internet-facing systems at European solar projects and wind farms that should not be reachable from the internet, including exposed admin interfaces and control panels.
The researchers mapped operating solar parks and wind farms in 40 countries across the European Union, the European Free Trade Association and EU candidate states, excluding rooftop installations, and found exposed systems in 35 of them. They presented the findings this week at the ONE Conference in The Hague.
Solar accounted for 7,942 of the systems, across 34 countries. Spain had 2,766, or 35% of the total, followed by Greece with 1,860, Italy with 753 and Germany with 672, according to Modat and the NCSC-NL. Those four countries account for 76% of exposed solar systems. Hungary had 514 and Turkey 454.
Wind accounted for 605 exposed systems in 23 countries, led by Germany with 212 and Italy with 192. Spain, which led the solar count, had only 11.
The researchers said the figures are likely an undercount, because systems were counted only once they could be confidently tied to specific sites. The count covers systems, not solar panels or wind turbines, and some of the systems found control several turbines or entire wind farms.
Start and stop
One example in the report is the web interface of a single wind turbine, reachable from the internet, showing live production data alongside start, stop and reset controls. Another page opens the web server of the Siemens programmable logic controller that runs the turbine, and a map page shows the turbine’s location. Other exposed login pages named the wind park they protected, and one noted that its default username was “root.”
Modat said it identified the systems with machine-learning clustering on its Magnify platform, which groups similar systems automatically and surfaced device types the researchers had not written search rules for. The researchers said attackers can map the same systems just as quickly. AI tools have already been used to
find remote shutdown weaknesses in microinverters
“What we can map in hours, an attacker can map in hours too. You can’t defend what you can’t see, and no one can see this whole landscape alone,” said Soufian El Yadmani, Modat’s founder and chief executive, who co-authored the report with NCSC-NL’s Bouke van Laethem.
The researchers published only aggregated country figures and did not name specific projects, operators or IP addresses. The affected parties are being informed through national computer emergency response teams. The report urges operators to take admin interfaces off the internet immediately, assume attackers are already inside their networks, and build visibility over the equipment that suppliers and service providers connect.
Thomas Plank, chief executive of Austrian industrial cybersecurity company Tributech, told
pv magazine
that taking the interfaces offline would not be enough, because unmanned, widely distributed sites must stay connected for grid operators, traders and maintenance contractors. “Today many can’t independently verify whether the data their control systems rely on is genuine or has been tampered with along the way,” said Plank.
Poland precedent
The report cites the
December 2025 attacks on Poland’s energy sector
, which hit at least 30 wind and solar farms. Poland’s national computer emergency response team, CERT Polska, found that attackers entered through internet-exposed firewall devices, many without multi-factor authentication, then used default credentials to disable remote terminal units, protection relays, operator workstations and communications equipment at grid connection substations.
The sites lost communication with distribution grid operators, though generation continued. CERT Polska attributed the attacks to a group associated with Russia’s Federal Security Service. The incident has since
exposed gaps in cyber insurance for battery storage
In 2025, cybersecurity company Forescout
found about 35,000 solar devices
with internet-exposed management interfaces, 76% of them in Europe. The European Union is also weighing
restrictions on inverters from high-risk suppliers
Renewables generated 54% of EU electricity in the second quarter of 2026, according to Eurostat, with solar providing 42% of that renewable output and wind 28%.
Italy, which ranked third in the Modat study’s solar-system count, has meanwhile introduced rules requiring solar and wind plants above 100 kW to
install central controllers that allow remote power control
, with deadlines running through 2028.

title: Plant diversity under PV modules rivals grassland at Japanese solar park - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers surveying a 55 MW solar plant on a former golf course in central Japan found that plant diversity under the panels was statistically indistinguishable from open grassland, with communities resembling forest edges, after five years of only twice-yearly mowing.
Brian Publicover
07 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Agrivoltaics
Utility-scale
A solar plant built on a former golf course in Japan’s heavily forested Gifu prefecture has developed diverse native vegetation under its panels without seeding or herbicides, according to a new study.
Japanese researchers Miharu Nakatani, Akira Noda and Takeshi Osawa surveyed the 169-hectare, 55 MW plant in the city of Gujo, operated by Pacifico Energy since July 2019. Apart from a commercial seed mix sown on exposed soil before operations began, the site has been managed only by mowing twice a year.
The team recorded 211 plant species from 54 families across 60 sample plots in summer and fall 2024, comparing five settings: under panels near the forest, under panels near open grassland, between panel rows, open grassland, and the surrounding forest edge.
They said that they did not find any significant difference in species richness or diversity between the five settings. However, species makeup did differ.
Vegetation under the panels resembled that of the forest edge, including shade-tolerant ferns, and differed most from the open grassland, where Miscanthus – a tall, fast-growing perennial grass – dominated. Non-native species covered less ground than native species in every setting, particularly under the panels, said the scientists.
Shade and shape
The researchers attribute the result to two key factors. Panel shade filtered out sun-loving grassland species and favored forest plants, and the plant’s intricate layout on steep terrain kept every point within about 200 meters of the forest, allowing seeds to disperse throughout the site. Even under-panel plots farther from the edge, about 85 meters on average, resembled forest-edge vegetation.
The scientists described the approach as “passive ecovoltaics,” in which solar plants become semi-natural habitat through natural succession and minimal maintenance rather than the active seeding used at many European and US sites. Earlier studies, largely in European farmland, have found lower plant diversity under panels.
The new Japanese model depends on a strong seed supply from surrounding land and a site shape that lets seeds reach its center, according to the scientists. They estimate that seed supply would likely be restricted where a facility’s center lies more than 1 km from its edge, and they warned against “greenwashing” where solar replaces grassland that supports rare or sun-loving species.
The study covers one site and one year of surveys and did not measure shade, moisture or soil conditions directly. The researchers are now calling for multi-year studies across several facilities.
Policy fit
The findings come as Japan increasingly tries to steer solar away from land conversion. Small- and medium-sized plants on forest land covered at least 84.7 square km in Japan by January 2020, about 59% of such installations, according to research cited by the scientists. Japan tightened forest development permits for solar in April, and new ground-mounted commercial solar will
lose feed-in support
Japan’s energy agency has
proposed four categories for continued priority solar support
but excluded former golf courses, ski resorts and abandoned farmland, citing the tree felling, topsoil removal and grading such projects can involve. The measures, published on Sept. 30, follow a
package of countermeasures on large-scale solar
approved in December 2025.
Panel shading is also at the center of Japan’s agrivoltaics rules. The Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF) plans to cap shading at 30%, a threshold the Japan Renewable Energy Foundation (JREF) has
called unreasonable
The scientists described their findings in “
Passive Ecovoltaics: Solar power plants as semi-natural ecosystems via spontaneous succession in forest landscapes
,” which was recently published in the
Journal of Environmental Management

title: Eskom extends solar registration fee waiver indefinitely  - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The South African utility is removing registration-related costs for grid-connected solar installations up to 50 kVA in size until further notice.
Patrick Jowett
07 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Residential
South Africa
South African utility
has extended its waiver of registration-related fees for small-scale solar systems until further notice.
Its grid connection fee waiver now applies to solar installations up to 50 kVA in size that are connected directly to its distribution network.
Eskom began campaigning for all South African customers with small-scale embedded generators up to 50 kW in size to register their solar installations in
early 2025
, initially offering an exemption on registration-related fees until March 2026.
The registration fee waiver was
then extended
until the end of last month, at which point Eskom announced its indefinite waiver.
The utility says the extension is made in the interest of safe grid integration and customer value while aligning with international best practice.
Its analysis of 20 international electricity markets across six continents found registration requirements are generally based on system capacity and become more rigorous as the size and complexity of installations increases.
Eskom’s latest update stresses that the waiver is designed to remove costs and provide additional time for customers to complete the registration process and does not change its underlying regulatory requirement for qualifying grid-connected generation facilities to be registered.
“Our focus is to make compliance clear, accessible and affordable,” commented Eskom Group Executive for Distribution Junaid Munshi.
“We want to assist customers with registering qualifying installations as simply as possible while supporting the safety of customers, contractors, employees and the broader electricity network,” Munshi added.
The utility’s statement also clarifies the waiver only applies to qualifying customers supplied directly by Eskom. Customers supplied by South African municipalities are advised to contact their licensed municipal redistributor regarding applicable registration requirements and charges.
In August, Eskom announced it would not go ahead with proposals to
fine customers with unregistered solar systems
South Africa’s cumulative solar capacity has surpassed 10 GW, after deploying
last year. The country is currently undergoing a
liberalisation of its energy market
with the phased introduction of its wholesale electricity market expected to begin early next year.

title: France's largest battery goes online - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
TagEnergy has inaugurated a 240 MW/480 MWh battery storage facility in northeastern France, the country’s largest operational BESS. The Tesla Megapack-based project provides grid-balancing services and is jointly owned by TagEnergy and Banque des Territoires.
Gwénaëlle Deboutte
07 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
TagEnergy has inaugurated a 240 MW/480 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) at Cernay-lès-Reims in northeastern France, making it the country’s largest operational battery storage project.
The project was inaugurated on Oct. 1 after four months of operation and is TagEnergy’s first operational storage asset in France. Since its founding in 2019, the Portuguese company has built a portfolio of more than 10 GW of solar, wind and battery storage capacity across the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Japan and Australia, with more than 2 GW currently operational.
Connected to transmission system operator RTE’s 225 kV grid, the project comprises 140 Tesla Megapack battery containers across just over 3 hectares. It entered operation after completing the simulations, tests and certifications required to provide frequency containment reserve, automatic frequency restoration reserve and voltage regulation services.
French construction and engineering group Eiffage carried out civil and electrical works, while Alsace-based photovoltaic and high-voltage engineering company Tewa Solar provided project management assistance from development through commissioning.
TagEnergy CEO Franck Woitiez said the Cernay-lès-Reims project shows that large-scale electricity storage has become an industrial reality in France. According to the company, the facility fed 70.5 GWh back into the grid during its first four months of operation and completed 145 full cycles over 125 days.
A banking consortium comprising ABN AMRO, NORD/LB and Caisse d’Épargne CEPAC provided financing for the project. TagEnergy jointly owns the facility with Banque des Territoires, which acquired a 49% stake in 2025, leaving TagEnergy as the majority shareholder.
The investment is the first under a three-year partnership between TagEnergy and Banque des Territoires aimed at financing several large-scale battery projects in France.
Banque des Territoires has invested in electricity storage since 2021 and currently has more than 250 MW of battery capacity in operation, 150 MW under construction and several hundred megawatts in development.
The financial institution said it plans to increase its involvement in the sector, which is expected to play a growing role in France’s decarbonized electricity system but continues to face challenges in securing bank financing due to the relative immaturity of battery storage business models.
